title: Exceptions: launch vs async, SupervisorJob, handlers
goal: By the end you can predict where a coroutine's exception goes (parent, await or handler), let independent work fail alone with a supervisor, put a CoroutineExceptionHandler where it actually runs, and spot the launch(SupervisorJob()) trap.

warmup.q: Inside `coroutineScope { }`, you start `val risk = async { riskScore(id) }` and then do 500 ms of other work before calling `risk.await()`. The risk call throws at 100 ms. When does anything happen?
options: Only at `await()`, at 500 ms: until then the exception waits inside the Deferred
At 100 ms: the scope is cancelled, the other work stops, and `coroutineScope` throws
Never: an exception in `async` is ignored unless someone awaits it
At 100 ms the exception is printed by the uncaught handler, and `await()` returns null
warmup.why: A failed child cancels its parent at once, and that is as true for `async` as for `launch`. The exception waits in the `Deferred` only when the parent is a supervisor or there is no parent. Here the scope is cancelled at 100 ms and `await()` is never reached.

analogy: Think of a coroutine family as a film crew on location. With a regular job, the crew is one unit: if the camera operator is injured, the director stops the shoot, sends everyone home and reports the incident to the studio. A supervisor is a courier depot instead. If one courier's van breaks down, the depot logs it and the other couriers finish their rounds, but when the depot closes for the night, everyone comes back. The exception handler is the depot's incident book: it records what went wrong after the fact and fixes nothing. `launch(SupervisorJob())` is hiring a freelancer through a different agency. They do the work, but your depot doesn't know they exist and won't call them back at closing time. The analogy breaks at the start of the trip: a real crew member can see the director wave. A coroutine only hears about a cancel at its next suspension point.
in_your_world: After a capture succeeds, a payments service usually fires several side effects: merchant webhooks, customer notifications, loyalty points, an analytics event. None of them should cancel the others, and none should fail the capture. If the request waits for them, wrap them in `supervisorScope` and turn each `await` into an outcome. If they run after the response, give a component one scope built with `SupervisorJob()`, `Dispatchers.IO` and a handler that logs with the payment id and increments a failure metric, and close it in `@PreDestroy`. The Kafka partition worker from lesson 3 of this track wants the same swap: with a `SupervisorJob`, one bad record no longer cancels every batch in the partition. And keep anything that must not be lost, such as the ledger write, out of fire-and-forget code entirely. It belongs in the request's own scope, or in an outbox table that a worker drains.
mistake: The most common mistake is trying to contain a failure at the wrong place: wrapping `await()` in `try` or `runCatching` inside `coroutineScope`, or putting a `CoroutineExceptionHandler` on a child `launch`. Both look like error handling, and neither runs before the damage is done, because a failed child cancels its parent the moment it fails. The scope and its other children are already cancelled when your `catch` would run, and the handler on a child is never consulted. Decide first whether the siblings should share a fate. If they should, let the failure propagate and catch it around the whole `coroutineScope`. If they shouldn't, use `supervisorScope` (or a scope with a `SupervisorJob`), and then a `try` around each `await` or a handler on the scope does work.

compare.title: A background sender: pool with an uncaught handler vs supervisor scope with a handler

java.title: WebhookSender.java

kotlin.title: WebhookSender.kt

compare.note: The two defaults are opposite. A Java thread pool is a supervisor without being asked: tasks never cancel each other, so you only have to make sure failures are seen (`execute` sends them to the uncaught handler, `submit` hides them in a `Future` nobody reads). A coroutine scope with a plain `Job` fails together, which is right for a request and wrong for a background sender, so you opt in with `SupervisorJob()`. After that the shapes match: `launch` is `execute` and goes to the handler, `async` is `submit` and keeps its failure for `await`. What Kotlin adds is the tree. The scope still knows every child, so `close()` cancels the sends in flight, and code that calls `post` from a test can wait for them.

steps.say: A capture handler posts a merchant webhook. The merchant's server was down, the webhook failure cancelled the ledger write, and someone fixed it like this. Tests became flaky (webhooks fire after the test has ended) and shutdown logs show webhooks posting into a closed HTTP client. Why?

The `SupervisorJob()` became the webhook's parent, so the webhook left the request's tree. Nothing waits for it and nothing cancels it. Decide what the author wanted. The response shouldn't wait for the merchant, so the webhook belongs to a long-lived owner. Give that owner a supervisor scope and a handler.
The capture goes back to a plain structured scope. The ledger write must succeed or fail with the capture, so it stays a child. The webhook is handed to its owner.
If the response must include whether the webhook got through, the request does wait, and the right shape is `supervisorScope` with an outcome per call instead.

Self-check: in step 4, the ledger write throws. What happens to the webhook call? (Nothing yet: it hasn't started. The exception is thrown from the `supervisorScope` block itself, so the scope is cancelled and rethrows. A supervisor protects siblings from each other, not from a failing block.)

lab.title: Notifications that fail one channel at a time
steps: Run the tests. Five of eight fail. `Notifications.kt` holds the shared model: `Channel`, `Sender` and `Outcome`.
In `NotifyAll.kt`, switch `coroutineScope` to `supervisorScope`, so a failed send stays in its own `Deferred`.
Give each send its own deadline with `withTimeoutOrNull(timeout)` inside the `async`, and map a `null` result to `Outcome.Failed("timed out")`.
Replace `runCatching` around `await()` with a `try` that rethrows `CancellationException` and turns any other exception into `Outcome.Failed(message)`. The notifyAll tests should now pass.
In `NotificationService.kt`, build the scope from `dispatcher + SupervisorJob() + handler`, where the handler calls `reportFailure` with the payment id from the coroutine's `CoroutineName`.
Run the tests until all eight pass. Then try `launch(SupervisorJob() + ...)` in `notifyLater` and see which tests catch it.
hints: `withTimeoutOrNull(timeout) { sender.send(paymentId) }` returns `Unit` when the send finishes and `null` when it times out.
`CoroutineExceptionHandler { context, error -> ... }` gets the failed coroutine's context, so `context[CoroutineName]?.name` is the payment id that `notifyLater` set.
A handler is used only by root coroutines. Children launched straight into a scope built with `SupervisorJob()` count as roots, so a handler in the scope's context sees their failures.
The `close` and `pending` tests already pass on the stub. They are there to catch the `launch(SupervisorJob())` trap.

alt.title: Java equivalent

recap: A failed child cancels its parent at once, whether it was started with `launch` or `async`, and whether or not anyone awaits it.
`launch` and `async` differ only at the root: a root `launch` goes to a `CoroutineExceptionHandler`, a root `async` keeps the exception for `await`.
`CoroutineExceptionHandler` runs only for root coroutines and direct children of a supervisor, never for `async`. It is for logging, not recovery.
A supervisor lets children fail alone, while cancellation still flows down. Use `supervisorScope` inside a function and `SupervisorJob()` in the constructor of a scope you own.
`launch(SupervisorJob())` replaces the parent and detaches the child from the tree. kotlinx.coroutines 1.11 deprecates passing a `Job` to builders.
When several children fail, the first exception wins and the rest are attached as suppressed.

options: `after` prints at 1 s, and the exception is lost because nobody awaited the `Deferred`
`after` never prints; at about 100 ms `coroutineScope` throws the `IOException`
`after` prints at 1 s, then `coroutineScope` throws the `IOException`
The uncaught exception handler prints the error, and `after` prints at 1 s
quiz.why: A failed `async` child cancels its parent immediately, exactly like `launch`. The scope's own `delay` is cancelled, `after` never prints, and the scope rethrows the child's exception. The "waits in the Deferred" behavior is only for supervisors and roots.

options: The handler logs the error and `coroutineScope` returns normally
The handler logs the error, then `coroutineScope` throws it too
The handler is ignored and `coroutineScope` throws the `IOException`
Nothing happens: the exception is swallowed by `launch`
quiz.why: The `launch` is a child, and a child hands its exception to its parent. Only roots consult a handler, so this one is never called. The scope fails and rethrows the exception to its caller.

quiz.q: A component sends merchant webhooks in the background for the whole life of the service. One failed webhook must not affect the others, failures must be logged, and shutdown must stop them. Which scope fits?
options: `CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.IO + handler)`, created once and cancelled on shutdown
`GlobalScope`, with `launch(handler)` for every webhook
`CoroutineScope(Job() + Dispatchers.IO)`, with `launch(SupervisorJob())` for every webhook
`supervisorScope { }` around each webhook, called from the request
quiz.why: A supervisor scope you own lets each webhook fail alone, routes failures to the handler, and still reaches every child on shutdown. `GlobalScope` and `launch(SupervisorJob())` detach the webhooks so nothing can cancel them, and `supervisorScope` in the request makes the request wait for the merchant.

options: `push sent` never prints; `supervisorScope` throws the `IOException`
`push sent` prints, then `supervisorScope` throws the `IOException`
Nothing prints: without a handler, the scope hangs
The uncaught exception handler prints the `IOException`, then `push sent` and `done` print
quiz.why: In a supervisor, a failed child doesn't cancel its sibling or the scope. A failed `launch` child has no `await`, so its exception goes to a handler, and with none installed it reaches the thread's uncaught exception handler, which prints it. The scope then returns normally after the slowest child.

quiz.q: From lesson 5 of this track: a notifier loops over channels with `try { sender.send(id) } catch (e: Exception) { log.warn("send failed", e) }`. During shutdown its scope is cancelled while SMS is being sent. What happens?
options: The loop stops at SMS, because `CancellationException` is not an `Exception`
The cancel is logged as a failed send, and each remaining channel is attempted and "fails" at once
The JVM interrupts the thread and the loop exits
The scope's handler receives the `CancellationException`
quiz.why: `CancellationException` extends `IllegalStateException`, so `catch (e: Exception)` catches it. The coroutine stays cancelled, so every later send throws at its first suspension point and is logged too. Rethrow `CancellationException` or catch narrower types. Handlers ignore cancellations.

flashcards.front: In a plain `coroutineScope`, an `async` child fails and nobody has called `await`. What happens?
flashcards.back: The scope is cancelled at once, its other children are cancelled, and the scope rethrows the child's exception.
On root coroutines and direct children of a supervisor. Never on ordinary children, never on `async`.
A failed child doesn't cancel its siblings or the scope. Cancelling the scope still cancels every child.

flashcards.front: A `launch` child of `supervisorScope` fails. Where does its exception go?
flashcards.back: To the `CoroutineExceptionHandler` in its context, or to the thread's uncaught exception handler if there is none.

flashcards.front: What does `launch(SupervisorJob()) { }` inside a scope really do?
flashcards.back: The new `SupervisorJob` becomes the parent, so the coroutine leaves the scope's tree: the scope doesn't wait for it or cancel it.
In the constructor of a scope you own: `CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + dispatcher + handler)`. Inside a function, use `supervisorScope { }`.

flashcards.front: Three children fail at once. Which exception does the parent rethrow?
flashcards.back: The first one. The other two are attached to it as suppressed exceptions.

terms.plain: A coroutine that ended with an exception other than CancellationException. It cancels its parent unless the parent is a supervisor.
A coroutine with no parent coroutine above it, such as one launched straight into a scope you created.
A context element that receives uncaught exceptions from root coroutines, for logging and metrics.
A job whose children fail independently. Cancellation still flows down to all of them.
The supervisor version of coroutineScope, for a block of work the caller waits for.
An extra failure attached to the first one, when several children fail together.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate asks why their `runCatching { quote.await() }` inside `coroutineScope` didn't stop one failed FX quote from failing the whole pricing call, and why moving a `CoroutineExceptionHandler` onto the `async` didn't help either. Explain, and say what you would write instead.
explain_back.answer: In a regular coroutineScope, a child that fails reports to its parent straight away, whether it's a launch or an async and whether or not anyone has awaited it. So the moment the quote failed, the scope was cancelled, the other quotes were cancelled, and coroutineScope rethrew the exception. The runCatching around await came too late to matter. The handler did nothing because handlers only run for root coroutines, and an async never uses one anyway: it keeps its exception for await. If one failed quote should not sink the others, use supervisorScope. There, a failed async child just stores its exception in its Deferred, so a try around each await, rethrowing CancellationException, turns each quote into a value or a failure. If the call really needs all the quotes, keep coroutineScope and catch the exception around the whole scope instead.

deeper.body:
`SupervisorJob(parent)` takes an optional parent, and that link works in one direction. If the parent is cancelled or fails, the supervisor is cancelled with it. A failure of one of the supervisor's children doesn't travel up. That makes `CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob(appJob) + dispatcher)` a good shape for a component scope that should die with the application but never take it down.

`supervisorScope` and `SupervisorJob` differ in one detail that bites in tests. `supervisorScope` waits for all its children, like `coroutineScope`, and rethrows if its own block throws. A scope built with `SupervisorJob()` never "completes" on its own: it is a long-lived container, and you end it with `cancel()`. That is why the lab's `NotificationService` has an explicit `close()`.

The last-resort path on the JVM is pluggable. kotlinx.coroutines looks up `CoroutineExceptionHandler` implementations through `ServiceLoader` and calls each of them before the thread's uncaught exception handler. kotlinx-coroutines-test uses that hook to collect exceptions from coroutines that escape the test, and since 1.7 `runTest` fails at the end if any were collected, even from coroutines that are not children of the test. That is why the lab's stub fails loudly instead of printing a stack trace and passing.

Finally, `CancellationException` again. Since a cancel is not a failure, it never goes to a handler, and a child that ends with it never cancels its parent. That is the rule that made the `runCatching` loop in lesson 5 of this track so dangerous, and it is also why `withTimeout` inside a `launch` fails quietly. Code that turns a timeout into a real error (`withTimeoutOrNull(d) { } ?: error("timed out")`) produces an `IllegalStateException`, which does travel up the tree.
